newsitem.title: GERMANY: Fresh questions arise over German EMU readiness.
newsitem.headline: Fresh questions arise over German EMU readiness.

text.p: Fresh questions were raised this weekend about Germany's ability to qualify for European monetary union by reports of a possible jump in the budget deficit and public resentment of the single currency project.
The respected weekly magazine Der Spiegel said the government itself sees a risk the country's 1997 budget deficit may post a surprising climb beyond the ceiling allowed for joining EMU.

Internal calculations at the Chancellor's office show the budget deficit climbing as high as 4.15 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, Der Spiegel said in a release ahead of publication on Monday.
A German government spokesman denied the report, saying the Chancellor's office had not made such calculations, but the article could still unnerve financial markets when trade opens on Monday.
The figure is well above the three percent level mandated by the Maastricht Treaty for joining monetary union and is also above the government's official target of 2.9 percent.
The German deficit stood at 3.8 percent last year.
Such a large deficit would mean that even under a liberal interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty, Germany would not be able to join the first wave of currency union planned for 1999.
EMU is scheduled to start on January 1, 1999, but the decision on who can join will be made in early 1998 on the basis of 1997 data.
A survey published on Saturday, meanwhile, showed that a majority of Germans are against EMU.
The Infratest Burke financial research institute said only 37 percent of Germans accepted the planned currency union, while 57 percent were against it, the Welt am Sonntag newspaper reported.

Of those against EMU, most were worried that the planned currency, the euro, would be weaker or less stable than the deutschemark, while others feared that Germany would end up carrying the financial burden of EMU.
Wilhelm Hankel, an adviser to former economics minister Karl Schiller, added his voice to the euro-doubters' chorus.
In a newspaper interview Hankel said Germany would fail to meet Maastricht Treaty deficit targets and that Europe could manage without adopting a single currency.
"One cannot pull the euro-train into the station if the roadbed is not stable," Hankel said.
Despite obstacles in meeting targets for monetary union, Finance Minister Theo Waigel would use the German budget to help Germany qualify, der Spiegel said.

The magazine said Waigel expects to be able to cut the apparent size of the budget deficit by calculating in a 10 billion mark surplus in pension contributions, eight billion marks from nursing care insurance and 1.75 billion marks in Bundesbank profits.
Government building projects, meanwhile, could be financed privately, allowing the government to put off actual spending to subsequent years.

Several members of the Bundesbank council have spoken out against using "accounting tricks" to qualify for monetary union, saying they would threaten confidence in the future European currency, the euro.
